study_identification_part.si3_author_journal_year: Coupé et al., Human Brain Mapping, 2022
study_identification_part.si4_title: Hippocampal-amygdalo-ventricular atrophy score: Alzheimer disease detection using normative and pathological lifespan models

cm1_research_objectives.reason: The study clearly states its research objectives. The purpose of applying normative modeling is described as developing an innovative MRI-based method for Alzheimer disease (AD) detection and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) prognosis using lifespan trajectories of brain structures. The study proposes a novel Hippocampal-Amygdalo-Ventricular Atrophy score (HAVAs) based on both normative lifespan models and AD lifespan models. The abstract explicitly mentions 'very accurate detection (AUC ≥ 94%) of patients with AD compared to control subjects and accurate discrimination (AUC = 78%) between progressive MCI and stable MCI'. The introduction provides detailed context comparing normative modeling with classification-based approaches and explaining the advantages of combining both strategies.
cm1_research_objectives.supporting_text: In this article, we present an innovative MRI-based method for Alzheimer disease (AD) detection and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) prognostic, using lifespan trajectories of brain structures... we propose a novel Hippocampal-AmygdaloVentricular Atrophy score (HAVAs) based on normative lifespan models and AD lifespan models... our approach showed very accurate detection (AUC ≥ 94%) of patients with AD compared to control subjects and accurate discrimination (AUC = 78%) between progressive MCI and stable MCI (during a 3-year follow-up).

(2) Preprocessing steps are mentioned in detail: image denoising (Manjón et al., 2010), inhomogeneity correction (Tustison et al., 2010), affine registration to MNI space, automatic quality control (QC) using RegQCNet, a second inhomogeneity correction in MNI space (Ashburner & Friston, 2005), and final intensity standardization step (Manjón & Coupé, 2016). nm8_normative_modeling_approach.reason: The study builds a NEW normative model and all three criteria are satisfied. (1) The type of statistical model is specified: polynomial models (linear, quadratic, cubic) are used to estimate volume trajectories. (2) Key model settings are described: model selection is based on F-statistic (p<.05), T-statistic for coefficients (p<.05), and Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) to choose among candidates. Confidence intervals at 95% are estimated. Specific formulas for the models are provided. (3) Software is mentioned: the analysis appears to use statistical modeling (though specific software like Matlab or R is not explicitly stated for the polynomial fitting, AssemblyNet is mentioned for preprocessing and segmentation).
nm8_normative_modeling_approach.supporting_text: To estimate the volume trajectories, we considered several low order polynomial models: Linear model, Quadratic model... Cubic model... a polynomial model was considered as a potential candidate only when simultaneously F-statistic based on ANOVA (i.e., model vs. constant model) was found significant (p < .05) and when all its coefficients were also significant using T-statistic (p < .05). Afterwards, to select the most relevant model between these potential candidates, we used the Bayesian Information Criterion (Schwarz, 1978). In addition, we estimated the distance between both AD and CN models as the Euclidean distance between trajectories. Finally, we estimated the confidence interval for each model at 95%

cr6_interpretation_of_deviation_scores.reason: All three criteria are satisfied. (1) The meaning and direction of deviation scores are explained: HAVAs score (S_AD) reflects the probability for the subject to be an AD patient, with scores normalized so that sum of CN and AD scores equals 1. The paper explains that 'when AD score is higher than 50%, the closest model is the AD model' and 'an AD score of 50% (i.e., CN score of 50%) is obtained for an equal distance between both models.' The formulas show how distances to CN and AD models are converted to probability scores. (2) Quantitative thresholds are reported: the decision boundary is 50% (the middle distance between both models), shown in Figure 3 as the orange curve. (3) Clinical implications are discussed extensively: relationships with classification performance (sensitivity, specificity, AUC) are provided; comparisons to other methods are made; the clinical utility for AD detection and MCI prognosis is discussed; and limitations are acknowledged (e.g., higher variability in AD patients).
cr6_interpretation_of_deviation_scores.supporting_text: we proposed new scores of being an AD patient (respectively a CN subject) based on the distance to the models. This score was built to ensure that when AD score is higher than 50%, the closest model is the AD model. Moreover, we ensured that an AD score of 50% (i.e., CN score of 50%) is obtained for an equal distance between both models... Consequently, the proposed HAVAs (i.e., the S_AD score) reflects the probability for the subject under study to be a patient with AD (or a pMCI subject)... The boundary decision is simply the middle distance between both models. Consequently, false positive are CN subjects (green dots) below orange curve and false negative are AD patients (red dots) above orange curve. Visually, we observed that AD patients exhibited higher variability than CN subjects.
